title: Way for AI (Fable) to decorate levels without it looking like slop?
author: Boof_Water
selftext:
I promise this isn’t out of laziness. Genuinely trying to see how much Claude can do itself without human intervention.

With that said, I’ve bought and downloaded hundreds of assets for it to use, but it just cannot get decoration down. AI slop, junk piles that make no sense, props that make no sense, multiple of the same thing, clipping things, etc. After many, many, many attempts (had it create a vault just for level design and architecture, the engine developed AI slop detectors \[clipping and floating detection, etc.\], other measures) to no avail. It just cannot place things in a way that seems normal, human-like, and/or appealing.

Anybody have a solution for this? Or do I need to just suck it up and use the editor I had it build? (Important piece of info, it’s a custom engine + editor that the game is running on, not Godot or Unity or Unreal. My buddy suggested this may be why; Claude insists that it can ‘see’ and edit way better in this custom engine.) Anyways, maybe I could have it make a skill..? Up for any suggestions.

comments.author: BoltVnderhuge
comments.body:
In a pixel game, I had it make an algorithm to procedurally generate maps following strict criteria for spacing/mixing assets, etc. 

Maybe if you can get it to outline the design, it will have more luck?

replies.author: Boof_Water
replies.body: Yeah, I pretty much did this over iterations, about 10 different times for one section of the map, 2-3 times for just a room. It failed so badly after all that work (prompting, time + tokens) that I didn’t touch it again for like a day or two out of frustration.

comments.author: heavy-minium
comments.body: You need screenshot, artwork, examples. Without it, the results will be much worse.

replies.author: Boof_Water
replies.body: You’re exactly right on this, and it even has examples *from the asset pack authors themselves*, usually shipped as scenes, but it just cannot get it. It literally assembles kits for me now, based on those scenes. But it cannot translate concepts from a fully decorated asset-room to my actual level.

replies.author: heavy-minium
replies.body: Have you tried an intermediate step in which you let the agent extract level-design rules from those sample scenes?

comments.author: FullPurchase7489
comments.body: I've tried to as well, specifically with Unity, but to no avail, if I ask it to decorate a scene, it simply does it wrong almost every single time lol, even when asked to fix and verify with camera shots, it will still fail D:

replies.author: Boof_Water
replies.body: Honestly, you not even having a solution and just coming here to say you experience it in Unity as well is helpful in and of itself. That confirms there’s nothing really wrong with the engine or editor; we just found a plateau of Claude’s abilities

comments.author: YKLKTMA
comments.body: Just remember that the LLM has less intelligence than a lizard, it does not understand anything and therefore is not able to solve aesthetic problems, so the only way to do this is to do it yourself

replies.author: Boof_Water
replies.body: Eh, this view was accurate maybe 2 years ago. Fable 5 just coded 3 million lines for me over a few weeks; I think we can logically concluded that, while it’s not human, it’s very obviously smarter than a lizard

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
Quality is not measured by the number of lines.
LLM has no intelligence at all, so even the primitive intelligence of a lizard is more advanced.

comments.author: derAres
comments.body: I am working on a three js 3rd person 3d game and it can decorate well. A flat for example. Told it to make it look like its full of ikea furniture. The placing was all good. What i did have to do was go through it and say „x looks not enough like a“ ….. or „what is y supposed to be“ the in the iterations it improved the 3d and so on.

replies.author: Boof_Water
replies.body: Yeah, see, but imagine that, but like 300 times for one small room filled with props. It’d just be easier to have it make sure everything is imported and put together, ready to drag-in with the editor

replies.author: derAres
replies.body: Another idea: simplify reporting issues to your ai. Here is what I did: have it build a report button in game that will capturw ny position and what i am looking at then i only wall throiugh the game and say „this is too simplistic“ and move on. Then intell claude „work through the new reports“. Saves a lot of time.

comments.author: pspahn
comments.body: Draft a ruleset for how things should be placed. Define what looks good. Make it follow your rules.

replies.author: Boof_Water
replies.body: Replied to another comment about this, but tl;dr is I did this, extensively, to no avail

replies.author: pspahn
replies.body:
You may have thought you did it, but you left too much agency to the agent. 

Quantify it. Imagine a forest. The things you know about the forest are the species generally found, their favored growing conditions, their abundance, etc. so you set rules. This thing typically grows on valley floors or this other thing grows on rocky slopes. All the things have their favorite places to be. 

Then cross reference those into a sort of multi element heat map, have rules for ratios, etc.

comments.author: ishmaellius
comments.body:
Honestly, anthropic models aren't good for anything visual.  They really just don't train on that dimension. 

If you can swing it, get a chatgpt subscription, and use it to generate concept art for your game. 

That gets you further along than Claude by itself. 

Lately I've been experimenting with using Codex to actually improve my games' visual fidelity as well to get it closer to concept art.  Seems to be working well, but I'm also quickly getting to the point I'll need to upgrade plans. 

The way I'd describe the difference is that Claude will think of coding things you don't necessarily specify that ultimately help in shipping better code.

I notice OpenAi's model does that same kind of thing, but in a visual sense for visual things.

replies.author: Boof_Water
replies.body:
This, now *this* is interesting. I’ve noticed Opus 4.8-5 are good at coding, Fable is incredible at coding and work delegation and *reasoning,* but it struggles with anything visual, period.

We’ve ironed that out through nights of improving the feedback loop in the engine editor - 40 screenshots per second for an AI that’s running it headless - but it made no difference.

So if you’re saying that ChatGPT is worth trying because it has better, visually-trained models that could potentially decorate levels like a human, than In all for trying it.

**But** if you’re saying that it would just be good to use for references and AI art generation, I can’t even really use it for that because, in order to keep the listing from being marked as having ‘AI generated content,’ I’m making 100% sure that it’s all 3D artist originated assets. Ridiculous, I know, but I think it’s gonna be pretty ironic when it comes out.

comments.author: teapot_RGB_color
comments.body:
To be honest I don't think we are there yet. 

The easiest way to deal with it is to make it work in phases, many phases. Start wide and narrow down. Create rules as you go, iterate a lot. Takes time.

comments.author: MagicGene
comments.body: I would try Codex for this. The new model has been quite effective at doing something very similar for my game.

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body:
Hey I'm building a level editor and was facing the same problem. 
What you need are pipelines and rules for every kind of asset type you plan to automatically place via llm. 
Claude doesn't know how perfect placement looks like to you. 

Take one asset group for example plants and give directions where and how you want them placed. 
Even better is if you have a screenshot how it's supposed to look. Just ask the ai to keep improving until the two look alike. 

This is how I achieve my artstyle without it looking generic (at least to me)

comments.author: Badnik22
comments.body:
Totally possible: get the AI to write a placement algorithm that follows whatever rules you want. Then run the algorithm.

For instance: voxelize your naked level geometry, then place props in a way that 1, 2 or 3 sides of their bounding box align with voxel boundaries. You coild give different probabilities for each of the 3 to control how many props in the middle of rooms, up against a wall, or in a corner.

comments.author: Extra-Ad5735
comments.body:
Do a level by hand (or by kicking Claude in the nuts until it ends up with desired result) then tell it use it as a learning sample for generating new levels, accounting for objects' relative positions to each other and to the environment. I.e. a pile of rubbish on the floor is allowed to only be on the floor, a wall light is only allowed on a wall, nicely spaced from neighbouring lights.

This is how some studios do this, by utilising a learning algorithm derived from Markov chains to quickly generate areas in the same style. You can actually ask Claude to implement that algorithm for you but I expect it will fail.

comments.author: PhotojournalistBig53
comments.body: It can build an OK baseplate. Had more success with codex than fable for that, but you need to set clear rules and give it screenshots, regardless I still always go through every inch of the map and fix, adjust, remove and add stuff. It gives you a great drawing board though and that's enough for me.
